intro: Most people in Durham start thinking seriously about a wet room when a family member's mobility changes, or when they're finally ready to tackle that cramped, dated bathroom that's been on the to-do list for years. A wet room replaces the traditional shower tray and screen with a fully tanked, level-access shower area — water drains away through a floor drain, and the whole space is designed to get wet. Done properly, it's a genuinely transformative bathroom upgrade that adds real value to your home. Durham properties lend themselves well to this kind of work, and local demand has grown steadily as homeowners look for both practical accessibility and that clean, contemporary finish.
localContext: Durham's housing stock is unusually varied, and the property type you're working with makes a real difference to how a wet room installation unfolds. Older stone-built properties and period cottages — common throughout the city and surrounding villages — tend to have solid floors, thick original walls, and sometimes unpredictable drainage routes that require careful planning before work starts. Suspended timber floors in these older homes need structural assessment before tanking, and some cottages have limited ceiling height that affects the choice of shower valve and overhead fittings. Modern estate properties on the outskirts of Durham are generally more straightforward, with regular joist spacing and accessible pipework, but they often have smaller bathroom footprints that require clever design. One genuinely useful point for Durham homeowners: the area is served by soft water from Pennine reservoirs, which means you won't see the heavy limescale buildup that plagues parts of Yorkshire or the South East. Soft water is kinder to shower screens, pumps, and valves, so maintenance costs over time tend to be lower — a practical advantage worth knowing when you're investing in a premium installation.
serviceDetail: A proper wet room installation in Durham follows a clear sequence of stages, and understanding them helps you manage expectations and spot whether a contractor is cutting corners. The process starts with a site survey — a good installer will assess your existing floor construction, check drainage fall possibilities, and discuss layout options before quoting. For older stone-built Durham properties this survey stage is especially important, as surprises behind walls or under floors are common. Once the design is agreed and materials ordered, the first physical stage is stripping out the existing bathroom completely. The subfloor is then prepared — either a screed is laid to create the correct fall toward the drain, or a purpose-made wet room former is used, which is faster and works well in both period and modern homes. Tanking comes next: a waterproof membrane is applied to the floor and walls, typically up to around 1.8 metres, and all joints and penetrations are sealed carefully. This is the most critical stage — poor tanking is the root cause of almost every wet room that causes damp problems later. Once the tank has cured, tiling or wall panels are fitted, the drain is set, and then the plumbing — shower valve, thermostatic controls, and any heated towel rail — is connected and tested. The final fix includes any glass screens, lighting, and sealant work. From start to finish, expect the installation to take between five and eight working days for a typical Durham bathroom.
pricing: Wet room installations in Durham typically fall in the range of £6,000 to £12,000 for a complete project, including design, labour, waterproofing, tiling, and quality fixtures. Where your project sits in that range depends on a few key factors. The size of the room matters, but so does the complexity — a stone-built Durham cottage with a solid floor and awkward drainage can cost more to prepare correctly than a modern estate bathroom of the same size. Your choice of finishes has a significant effect: standard tiles and a quality thermostatic valve sit at the lower end, while large-format porcelain, designer shower fittings, and underfloor heating push costs toward the top. A walk-in glass screen, a fold-down shower seat, or a ceiling-mounted rainfall head all add to the total but are frequently requested in Durham installations.
whyLocal: Hiring a Durham-based installer rather than a regional firm covering a wide area pays dividends on a project like this. Local tradespeople will have worked in the specific property types you find in Durham — they'll know the quirks of solid stone floors in older city-centre cottages, the pipework conventions on newer estates, and which suppliers can get materials to site quickly. They're also easier to reach if a small snag appears after completion. Word of mouth still travels fast in a city the size of Durham, and experienced local installers have a direct incentive to do work they're proud of. Ask for examples of completed wet room projects in the local area and speak to previous clients where possible.

faqs.q: Can a wet room be installed in an older stone-built Durham property with a solid floor?
faqs.a: Yes, and solid floors are actually well-suited to wet room installation — there's no need to worry about the structural implications for timber joists. The main consideration is achieving adequate fall toward the drain, which may require screeding. A good installer will assess drainage options during the survey and advise on the most practical approach for your specific property.

faqs.q: How long does a wet room installation take in Durham?
faqs.a: Most wet room projects in Durham take between five and eight working days from strip-out to completion. Older properties occasionally extend this timeline if unexpected issues arise during preparation — discovering a compromised subfloor or an awkward drainage route can add a day or two. Your installer should give you a realistic programme after the site survey, not before it.

faqs.q: Does the soft water supply in Durham affect how a wet room performs long-term?
faqs.a: It's actually a benefit. Durham's soft Pennine water supply means limescale doesn't build up on shower heads, valves, or glass screens the way it does in harder water areas. Your wet room will be easier to maintain and components should have a longer working life. It's still worth fitting a quality thermostatic valve, but you're unlikely to need a water softener or specialist descaling treatments.

faqs.q: Will a wet room add value to my Durham home?
faqs.a: A well-designed, professionally installed wet room generally adds value, particularly in Durham's market where period and character properties command premium prices. Buyers increasingly expect high-quality bathrooms, and a level-access wet room appeals both as a lifestyle feature and for accessibility reasons. Poor installation — especially inadequate waterproofing — can have the opposite effect, which is why choosing an experienced installer matters.
